subject: Science
chapter: Chapter 9: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life
central_question: How can differences in the properties of mixture components help us choose one or more suitable methods of separation?
in_scope_units: Understanding why useful and unwanted components are separated in everyday life
Using handpicking to remove visibly different unwanted pieces
Separating grain from stalks by threshing
Separating lighter husk from heavier grain by winnowing
Using sieving when solid particles differ in size
Recovering dissolved salt from water by evaporation
Allowing insoluble solids to settle and separating liquid by sedimentation and decantation
Using cloth, strainers and filter paper for filtration
Separating butter from curd by churning
Using a magnet to separate magnetic material from a non-magnetic mixture
Selecting and combining methods for mixtures with several components
banned_topics: Detailed distillation apparatus and fractional distillation
Municipal water-treatment processes beyond the simple filter model in the chapter

known_pitfalls.claim: Threshing and winnowing are the same method.
known_pitfalls.correction: Threshing separates grains from stalks, while winnowing uses moving air to separate lighter husk from heavier grain.

known_pitfalls.claim: Filtration can remove dissolved salt from water.
known_pitfalls.correction: Dissolved salt passes through an ordinary filter with the water; evaporation is used to recover the salt.

known_pitfalls.claim: Sieving works for any two solid materials.
known_pitfalls.correction: Sieving is useful when the particles have a suitable difference in size so that smaller particles pass through the sieve openings.

known_pitfalls.claim: A clear filtrate is automatically safe to drink.
known_pitfalls.correction: Filtration can remove visible insoluble particles, but clarity alone does not prove that water is safe for drinking.

recommended_example_progression: Distinguish handpicking, threshing and winnowing using the opening grain example.
Compare sieving and evaporation using the flour-and-bran and salt-from-seawater examples.
Explain sedimentation, decantation and filtration using the tea, muddy-water and oil-water observations.
Explain churning and magnetic separation using the curd and iron-nail examples.
Select and combine methods for multi-component mixtures.
